offices.name: Quaestor
offices.description: Keeper of the treasury and the army's pay chest. The first rung of the ladder, taken young, and the only one where honest bookkeeping is expected.
offices.historical_basis: The quaestorship was the entry magistracy of the Roman cursus honorum. Quaestors kept the state treasury at Rome and served as paymasters and deputies to consuls and provincial governors in the field, and the censors filled the Senate largely from men who had held it. Four served each year in the early Republic; the college grew as Rome's business did, to eight in the third century BC and to twenty under Sulla, who also set a minimum age near thirty.

offices.name: Aedile
offices.description: Master of streets, markets, grain and games. He spends his own fortune on spectacles so the crowd remembers his name when he stands again.
offices.historical_basis: Four aediles served each year from 367 BC, two plebeian and two curule. They maintained the public buildings, streets and water supply of Rome, policed its markets and weights, watched over the grain supply and staged the public games. Ambitious men financed those games lavishly from their own purses to buy popularity for the offices above; Caesar's aedileship of 65 BC, which left him deep in debt, is the notorious example.

offices.name: Praetor
offices.description: Judge of the city and, when the year demands it, a general. He holds imperium, the right to command in the field.
offices.historical_basis: The praetorship was created in 367 BC and carried imperium. The urban praetor presided over the courts at Rome; a second praetor, for cases involving foreigners, was added about 242 BC, and the college reached six by 197 BC as the provinces multiplied. Praetors commanded armies and governed provinces when the consuls were elsewhere. The two seats here stand for the college of the mid-third century.

offices.name: Pontifex Maximus
offices.description: Highest priest of the state cults, chosen for life. The gods speak through him, which makes him very hard to argue with.
offices.historical_basis: The pontifex maximus headed the college of pontiffs, kept the calendar and the sacred law, and held the office for life; it stood outside the annual ladder of magistracies. From the third century BC he was chosen by a special assembly of seventeen of the thirty-five tribes rather than co-opted by the college. Publius Licinius Crassus Dives won it in 212 BC before holding any curule office; Caesar won it in 63 BC, at thirty-seven, by bribery on a scale that alarmed his creditors. Here the priesthood is kept until death and its holder stands for nothing else.

offices.name: Consul
offices.description: One of the two heads of the Republic for a year. Armies, honors and enemies follow the office, and the year is named for him.
offices.historical_basis: Two consuls, elected each year by the centuriate assembly, held the supreme civil and military authority of the Republic and gave their names to the year. The lex Villia annalis of 180 BC fixed the ladder beneath the consulship, with the praetorship before it and set intervals between offices; its schedule made forty-two the consular year, which Sulla later re-enacted. The earlier Republic knew consuls in their thirties.

offices.name: Censor
offices.description: Counter of citizens, judge of morals, letter of the public contracts. One stroke of his stylus can strike a man from the rolls.
offices.historical_basis: Two censors were elected at roughly five-year intervals, normally from among former consuls, to hold the census, assign citizens to their classes and tribes, revise the roll of the Senate by expelling the unworthy, and let the state's contracts. The office ran eighteen months and ranked above the consulship in dignity; it was the crown of a senatorial career. Here the pair is refilled each summer with the rest of the ladder.
